metadata.title: Recommend, Not Install.
metadata.subtitle: The Claude Automation Recommender Skill
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: when you ask Claude to look at your codebase and suggest Claude Code automations, does it build them for you — or does it stop somewhere short of that? Lands the carry-out that the skill recommends and explains, but never creates a file, and doesn't always hand you the exact command either.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. Claude Code's extensibility surface has five slots, and each one answers a different question about triggering and scope. Hooks are event-driven — they fire automatically on tool events: format on save, block a risky edit, run tests after a change. Subagents are specialized workers Claude can spawn in parallel — a code reviewer, a security auditor, a test writer. Skills are packaged workflows Claude invokes on request, or you fire yourself with a slash command. Plugins bundle related skills for one-step install. MCP servers reach outside Claude entirely — databases, APIs, browsers, documentation. Five slots, five triggers, five scopes. The design forces you to pick the right shape for the job instead of stretching one generic hook into everything.

The mechanism is three phases. First, it reads your codebase — package files for language and framework, existing Claude config, test setup, CI files, database and API code. Second, it matches what it found to a specific recommendation, one automation type at a time, then caps it — one or two per category, the single most valuable pick, not everything possible; and it tells you that you can ask for more. Third, it writes a report — your codebase profile, then one section per automation type, each with what to add, why it fits, and how to install it. Prettier configured means a format-on-save hook. A GitHub repo means the GitHub MCP server. Code touching auth or payments means a security-reviewing subagent. They optimized for signal density over completeness — the cap is the design's honest answer to the fact that you don't need every possible automation, you need the two that actually pay off.

beats.narration_text: Here's the catch, and it's a design decision, not a bug. Recommending is not the same as handing you a runnable step. For a subagent, the skill points at a template file instead of writing the scaffold inline. For a plugin, it names the plugin but skips the install command — that's still a separate lookup. It's read-only end to end: it never edits your files, and it never finishes that last step either. This works if you value your own hand on the tiller — nothing gets installed you didn't type out. It fails if you were hoping the recommendation would just execute itself. The distance between 'here's what to add' and 'here's the exact command' is yours to close, on purpose.
It analyzes your codebase and tells you what to add and why — it never creates a file, and it doesn't always hand you the exact command to run either. Recommending isn't installing.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, in any real project: Analyze this codebase and recommend Claude Code automations. Then check two things the recommender doesn't hand you finished. For any subagent it suggests, does it write the actual agent file, or just point at a template? For any plugin, does it give you the exact install command, or just the plugin's name? The gap between the recommendation and the runnable step is where the design lives.

props.command: Analyze this codebase and recommend Claude Code automations.

beats.narration_text: Here's a prompt you can paste straight into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Ask it to take Claude Code's five extension types apart — hooks, subagents, skills, plugins, and MCP servers — and, for each one, name what triggers it, what scope it runs in, one honest case where it's the right choice, and one honest case where a different type would fit better. Don't let it sell them; make it evaluate them on their own terms. Go deeper: what would a sixth automation type do that the current five can't, and what would you have to sacrifice in the design to make it fit alongside the others?

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to understand Claude Code's extension surface. There are five extension types — hooks, subagents, skills, plugins, and MCP servers — and each one has a different trigger and scope. For each of the five, explain (1) what event or gesture triggers it, (2) what scope it operates in (a single tool call, a whole session, outside Claude entirely), (3) one honest example where it's the right choice, and (4) one honest case where a different type would be a better fit. Don't sell them — evaluate them on their own terms, and name the trade-off each one makes.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: If you had to design a sixth automation type that filled a gap the current five don't cover, what would it do, what would trigger it, and what would you have to sacrifice in the design to make it fit alongside the others?
